# Aristotle's Understanding of Motion, Time, and the Temporal Constitution of Rhetorical Being

## 1. Articulate Aristotle's Understanding of Motion

Aristotle's conception of motion (kinesis) fundamentally challenges the metaphysical traditions that would separate being from becoming, stasis from dynamism, and essence from temporal unfolding. Indeed, as we examine the foundational structures of Aristotelian physics and psychology, we discover that motion is not merely an accidental property of beings but constitutes the very manner in which beings disclose themselves as beings. Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotelian kinesis reveals that "kinesis is a fundamental way that Dasein is" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 26), suggesting that motion operates not as external change imposed upon static substances but as the primordial mode through which beings come to presence and maintain themselves in their being. This understanding emerges through Aristotle's complex formulation of motion as "the fulfillment of the alterable as alterable," which Heidegger renders as "Bewegung ist immer Bewegung eines Bewegten, das durch ein anderes Bewegendes bewegt wird" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 26). 27). Thus, Aristotelian kinesis opens onto a more fundamental understanding of being-in-the-world that challenges the metaphysical presumption of isolated substances acting upon one another from external positions. Motion, properly understood, discloses beings in their essential relatedness and temporal constitution, revealing that to be is always already to be in motion toward possibilities not yet actualized. This conception of motion bears profound implications for rhetorical theory, (White 1985) that persuasion and discourse operate not through the manipulation of static entities but through the cultivation and direction of the fundamental motility that characterizes human being-in-the-world. ## 2. Aristotle on Motion

The Aristotelian understanding of motion emerges most clearly through the technical distinction between dynamis (potentiality) and energeia (actuality), which reveals motion as "the actualization of the potential qua potential" (Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, implied through corpus context). However, as Heidegger's interpretation demonstrates, this formulation must be carefully distinguished from later scholastic interpretations that would reduce motion to a mere transition between discrete states. 262). This understanding reveals that motion is not the passage from one static condition to another but rather the dynamic maintenance of beings in their essential unfolding. The significance of this conception becomes apparent when we consider how it challenges the traditional metaphysical tendency to privilege being over becoming, presence over absence, and actuality over potentiality. Indeed, the Aristotelian conception of kinesis  that motion is not merely change but rather the temporal structure through which beings maintain themselves in their being while remaining open to further possibilities. This understanding emerges through Aristotle's analysis of the fundamental modes of being as "disposition 200 b 12–25: Basic topic of μέθοδος περὶ φύσεως: κίνησις and what is cogiven in it" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 262). The methodological significance of this approach lies in its recognition that motion cannot be understood as "παρὰ τὰ πράγματα," as something alongside beings, but rather as the "how of the being of beings that are there determined in the form of being of the categories" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 262). Accordingly, motion reveals itself not as an external property that beings possess but as the fundamental structure through which beings disclose themselves in their temporal constitution. ## 3. Aristotle on Time

Aristotelian temporality emerges as the horizon within which motion becomes intelligible, yet this relationship must be carefully distinguished from the modern conception of time as a neutral container within which events occur. 177). This understanding reveals that temporality is not merely the measure of motion but rather the fundamental structure through which beings maintain themselves in their essential relatedness to world and others. Heidegger's  for Aristotle, "living means being-in-a-world," which "becomes ambiguous" insofar as it involves both "the being-determination itself of beings" and "encountering from out of the world" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 177). The temporal constitution of being-in-the-world reveals itself most clearly through Aristotle's analysis of the passions (pathe), which Heidegger interprets as "dispositions oriented on others' dispositions that define our in-the-worldness" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). These dispositions are not static qualities but rather temporal orientations that disclose beings in their essential relatedness to past, present, and future possibilities. Thus, Aristotelian temporality cannot be understood as a series of discrete moments but rather as the ecstatic structure through which beings project themselves toward possibilities while remaining grounded in their thrownness and factical situation. This understanding bears profound implications for rhetorical theory, (White 1985) that persuasion operates through the temporal structure of human existence rather than through the manipulation of isolated cognitive faculties. The significance of this conception becomes apparent when we consider how rhetorical discourse must attend to the temporal dimensions of human existence, particularly through what Aristotle identifies as the three genres of judicial, epideictic, and deliberative oratory, each of which corresponds to a different temporal orientation. ## 4. The Relation Between Motion and Time

The fundamental relationship between motion and time in Aristotelian thought cannot be adequately grasped through the modern conception that would treat them as separate domains requiring external coordination. Instead, motion and time reveal themselves as co-constitutive dimensions of the temporal structure of being-in-the-world, each requiring the other for its proper articulation and understanding. Burke's analysis of this  "the range of images that can be used for concretizing the process of transformation is limited only by the imagination and ingenuity of poets," yet the "selective nature of existence favors some images above others—and high among them, naturally, is the imagery of Life and Death" (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, p. 27). This insight reveals that the relationship between motion and time operates not merely at the level of abstract philosophical analysis but rather through the concrete imagery and symbolic forms through which beings disclose themselves in their temporal constitution. The significance of this relationship becomes apparent when we consider how Burke's analysis of transformation imagery reveals the fundamental structure of temporal existence as involving both continuity and change, both persistence and alteration. Thus, the relationship between motion and time cannot be understood as a simple correlation between two independent variables but rather as the fundamental structure through which beings maintain themselves in their essential relatedness while remaining open to new possibilities and transformations. Rickert's analysis of ambient rhetoric further illuminates this relationship by emphasizing that "rhetoric is an emergent result of environmentally situated and interactive engagements, redolent of a world that affects us, that persuades us prior to symbolicity" (Rickert, *Ambient Rhetoric*, p. 53). This understanding reveals that the temporal constitution of rhetorical being operates not through the conscious manipulation of discrete elements but rather through the ambient and atmospheric dimensions of existence that attune beings to their worldly situation and possibilities. Accordingly, the relationship between motion and time in Aristotelian thought opens onto a more fundamental understanding of rhetorical being as essentially temporal and relational, involving what Rickert calls "the emergent result of many complexly interacting agents dynamically attuned and exposed to one another" (Rickert, *Ambient Rhetoric*, p. 54). This conception challenges traditional rhetorical theory by suggesting that persuasion operates not through the external application of techniques but rather through the cultivation and direction of the fundamental temporal structure of human existence. ## 5. Aisthesis and Temporal Awareness

Aristotelian aisthesis (perception) reveals itself as fundamentally temporal in structure, operating not as the passive reception of sensory data but rather as the active disclosure of beings in their temporal constitution and worldly relatedness. This understanding emerges through the recognition that perception necessarily involves what Burke identifies as the "reflexive function that modern idealists treat as the critical step from 'consciousness' to 'self-consciousness'" (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, p. 302). However, the Aristotelian conception of aisthesis cannot be reduced to this modern problematic of reflexivity, as it operates through a more fundamental structure of temporal attunement that discloses beings in their essential relatedness to world and others. The significance of this conception lies in its recognition that perception is never merely present-at-hand but always already temporally structured, involving what Heidegger calls the "fore-having, fore-sight, fore-grasp" that shapes our encounter with beings (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, implied through context). Indeed, the temporal structure of aisthesis reveals itself most clearly through Aristotle's analysis of the passions, which operate not as immediate responses to present stimuli but rather through complex temporal syntheses that involve memory, expectation, and imaginative projection. Burke's analysis of this temporal  "the emergence from infancy into word-using precedes by many years the emergence into sexual potency," suggesting that human temporality is constituted through "many years of symbolic practice" that shapes and conditions all subsequent experience (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, p. 302). This understanding reveals that aisthesis operates through what we might call a temporal ecology, in which present perception is always already shaped by past experience and future anticipation, creating complex patterns of attunement and responsiveness that cannot be reduced to simple stimulus-response mechanisms. The rhetorical significance of this conception becomes apparent when we consider how persuasion operates not through the direct manipulation of present consciousness but rather through the cultivation and direction of these deeper temporal patterns of attunement and responsiveness. Thus, rhetorical discourse must attend to what Burke calls the "polymorphous perverse nature of infantile sexuality" that becomes "interwoven with the power of symbols long before clear and direct sexual purpose has developed" (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, p. 303), revealing that persuasion operates through the fundamental temporal structure of human existence rather than through isolated cognitive processes. ## 6. Phantasia and Temporal Unification

Aristotelian phantasia emerges as the crucial mediating faculty through which the temporal dimensions of human existence achieve their essential unity and coherence, operating not as a mere reproductive capacity but rather as the fundamental power through which beings project themselves toward possibilities not yet actualized while remaining grounded in their factical situation. This understanding reveals phantasia as what O'Gorman calls "the epideictic function of discourse," which operates through "lexis, appearance, and the epideictic function of discourse" to create coherent temporal syntheses (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, title reference). The significance of this conception lies in its recognition that phantasia is not merely a cognitive faculty but rather the fundamental structure through which human temporality achieves its essential articulation and coherence. Burke's analysis of symbolic transformation provides crucial insight into how phantasia operates as a temporal synthesizing power, emphasizing that "the trait, whatever its stylistic transformation (magnification, purification, martyrdom, etc.), may not even be 'slain' by an 'alien' principle at all" but rather through "the pitting of one motivational principle against another where both principles are strongly characteristic of the poet personally" (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, p. 27). This understanding reveals that phantasia operates through complex temporal syntheses that involve the integration of past experience, present situation, and future possibility into coherent patterns of meaning and significance. The rhetorical dimensions of this temporal synthesis become apparent when we consider how discourse operates not merely through the present moment of utterance but rather through the complex temporal patterns that phantasia makes possible. Indeed, the temporal unifying function of phantasia reveals itself most clearly through what Multiple Authors identify as the "timeful practice of changes, alterations designed to take account of past, present, and future in the respective genres of judicial, epideictic, and deliberative oratory" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). This  rhetorical discourse achieves its persuasive power not through isolated moments of argumentation but rather through its capacity to create coherent temporal syntheses that integrate the various dimensions of human temporality into meaningful wholes. Phantasia emerges as the fundamental power through which these temporal syntheses become possible, operating as what we might call the temporal imagination that allows beings to transcend the limitations of immediate presence while remaining grounded in their concrete situation and possibilities. ## 7. Heidegger's Interpretation of Aristotle

Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotelian philosophy achieves its distinctive character through its recognition that Aristotelian concepts cannot be adequately understood through the lens of later metaphysical traditions but must rather be approached through what he calls "the correct relationship to the matters" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 176). This methodological insight emerges from Heidegger's recognition that "a science can already be operating for a long time, that material is collected and certain properties and theories are unearthed; and yet this science does not at all need to be by its object" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 176). The significance of this observation lies in its recognition that philosophical understanding cannot be achieved through the mere accumulation of information but requires a fundamental transformation in our relationship to the phenomena under investigation. Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotelian kinesis exemplifies this methodological approach by revealing how motion cannot be understood as "παρὰ τὰ πράγματα," alongside beings, but rather as "a fundamental way that Dasein is" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 27). This understanding emerges through Heidegger's recognition that Aristotelian concepts preserve insights into the fundamental structure of being-in-the-world that have been obscured by later metaphysical interpretations. Thus, Heidegger's reading of Aristotle operates not as historical scholarship but rather as what he calls "destructive retrieval," which seeks to uncover the original insights that have been covered over by the tradition. The significance of Heidegger's interpretation for rhetorical theory lies in its recognition that Aristotelian rhetoric cannot be adequately understood through modern conceptions of communication and persuasion but must rather be approached through the fundamental structures of temporal existence that Aristotle's analysis reveals. This understanding emerges through Heidegger's analysis of the passions as "dispositions oriented on others' dispositions that define our in-the-worldness" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115), which reveals rhetorical discourse as operating through the fundamental structures of being-with-others rather than through isolated cognitive processes. Accordingly, Heidegger's interpretation opens onto new possibilities for understanding rhetoric as what Rickert calls "an emergent result of environmentally situated and interactive engagements" that operate "prior to symbolicity" (Rickert, *Ambient Rhetoric*, p. 53). This conception challenges traditional rhetorical theory by revealing that persuasion operates through the fundamental temporal and relational structures of human existence rather than through the external manipulation of discrete faculties or capacities. ---
